Describe a reading configuration

Source: R/doc-read-spec.R
gr_read_spec.Rd

Describe a reading configuration

Usage

gr_read_spec(
  reader = "map_reduce",
  model = NULL,
  temperature = NULL,
  max_answer_tokens = 1500L,
  max_chunk_tokens = 700L,
  max_summary_tokens = 500L,
  top_k = 6L,
  min_score = -Inf,
  mmr = 1,
  context_order = c("relevance", "document", "edges"),
  rerank_candidates = 20L,
  rerank_min_score = 4,
  fan_in = 5L,
  max_levels = 5L,
  max_rounds = 4L,
  preview_tokens = 1200L,
  restate = c("auto", "always", "never", "window"),
  members = NULL,
  cite = FALSE,
  skim_model = NULL,
  summary_model = NULL,
  parallel = NULL,
  delay_between_calls = 0,
  on_overflow = c("warn", "error"),
  effort = NULL,
  premise = FALSE,
  verify = FALSE,
  accept_near_verbatim = FALSE,
  max_merge_levels = 6L,
  restate_tokens = 1200L,
  bm25_k1 = 1.5,
  bm25_b = 0.75,
  lexical_blend = 0.5,
  unskip_k = 0L,
  reread_on = c("never", "not_found"),
  low_score = c("not_found", "read_top_k"),
  fusion = c("default", "rrf"),
  rrf_k = 60,
  answer_format = c("parsed", "schema"),
  premise_verdict = c("sentence", "structured"),
  context_policy = NULL,
  refine_state = c("draft", "ledger"),
  effort_mode = c("static", "escalate"),
  ...
)

Arguments

reader

Reader name; see gr_readers().

model

Chat model id. NULL (the default) means the model of the client the spec is read with, so hr_client(model = "gpt-4o-mini") is the model that answers, is budgeted for and is billed. A model named here, or in a recipe, is used whatever the client's.

temperature

Sampling temperature, or NULL to omit the field. You do not need to null it yourself for reasoning models: it is dropped automatically for any model whose registry entry has supports_temperature = FALSE, which includes the default model. Check with hr_model_info(model)$supports_temperature.

max_answer_tokens

Output cap for final answers and merges.

max_chunk_tokens

Output cap for per-chunk calls.

max_summary_tokens

Output cap for summarisation calls.

top_k

For retrieve, rerank and iterative: chunks to use.

min_score

For retrieve: chunks scoring below this are dropped, but if that would leave nothing the single best chunk is used anyway. -Inf disables the filter. Not a cosine similarity when embeddings fall back to lexical vectors: the score is then a blend of cosine and BM25, and under fusion = "rrf" it is the fused score (see fusion). When no chunk passes, the answer's notes$below_min_score is TRUE.

mmr

Diversity of selection, for retrieve and iterative. 1 (the default) is plain top-k. Below 1, chunks are picked greedily by mmr * relevance - (1 - mmr) * similarity to what is already picked, so three chunks saying the same thing do not all get in and pay for each other. Costs nothing: the vectors are already computed. 0.7 is a reasonable place to start; 0 selects for novelty alone and will happily pick irrelevant chunks because they are different.

context_order

Where the selected chunks sit in the prompt. "relevance" (default) is most relevant first; "document" restores the order they appear in the document, which reads better when chunks are consecutive; "edges" puts the strongest first and second-strongest last, burying the weakest in the middle, because transformers attend measurably better to the beginning and end of a long context than to its middle. Selection is unaffected. This decides only placement, and it applies to retrieve, rerank and iterative, the readers that put several ranked chunks in one prompt. Under a context_policy with order_merges = TRUE it also places the findings map_reduce, skim and the write-up merge combine and the member answers ensemble adjudicates. These have no relevance order, so "relevance" and "document" keep the order they come in (document order for findings, member order for an ensemble), and "edges" puts the first first and the second last.

rerank_candidates, rerank_min_score

For rerank: how many chunks to score, and the score below which a chunk is discarded. The candidates are the chunks the word-matching prefilter ranks highest. When no chunk shares a word with the question, it cannot rank them, so they are picked by embedding similarity instead, or, when embeddings cannot rank them either, spread evenly over the document and the answer marked partial. Either way the run warns (gr_rerank_prefilter) and notes$prefilter says which.

fan_in, max_levels

For hierarchical: summaries combined per call, and the recursion depth cap.

max_rounds

For iterative: retrieve-assess cycles.

preview_tokens

For preview: the cap on the outline the planner sees. The outline is built from section labels, sizes and short excerpts (never the full text), and per-section excerpts shrink until the whole thing fits, so every section stays visible to the planner rather than the outline being truncated and some sections never being offered to it at all. The planner is an LLM call about a long document and so prone to exactly the degradation this package manages; keeping its input small is the mitigation.

restate

Whether to repeat the question before the excerpts as well as after them: "auto" when the body is long enough to bury the first ask, "always", or "never". "window" repeats it once the excerpts pass the length the model attends to reliably, its effective window; no model's effective window is measured yet, so it repeats the question before excerpts longer than 50,000 tokens and warns (gr_window_unmeasured). A setting rather than a rule, because whether it helps is a question about your corpus and your model. Point gr_compare() at two recipes differing only in this and find out.

members

For ensemble: the reader names to combine.

cite

Ask for chunk-level citations ([chunk 3]) in the answer. Map those ids back to pages via ans$evidence. Forced off for hierarchical, which answers from summaries: summaries carry no [chunk N] ids, so asking for citations there asks the model to invent them. For skim, when its evidence has to be consolidated to fit and no [chunk N] label survives the consolidation, citations are not asked for either (notes$cite_dropped = TRUE); when some survive, a citation is checked against those.

skim_model, summary_model

Optional cheaper models for the per-chunk stages. skim_model is used by skim's extraction and rerank's relevance scoring; summary_model by hierarchical's summarisation.

parallel

Run per-chunk calls in parallel. Needs the future and future.apply packages; without them the run is sequential and says so.

The trace is complete either way: workers keep their own and the parent absorbs them, in input order, so a parallel run reports the same calls, tokens and cost as the same run made sequentially. So is what the client keeps: a mock's or backend's $calls() and $embeds(), and the hit, miss and write counts of an attached cache, include the calls made in workers, added back in input order. A replay client always runs one request at a time, since it hands out its recording in order.

Two things do not cross the process boundary. The limits in hr_options() are checked before a batch is sent and not inside it, since a worker cannot see what the others spend. So the pre-flight check, which runs in the parent, holds a parallel run to its worst case, every reply at its cap and as many merge or summary levels as replies that size need, against both max_calls and max_cost_usd; and each batch goes to the workers only when it fits what the run has left at its own worst case, and otherwise runs one request at a time, each checked. And a handler that records calls in variables of its own (a closure passed to hr_backend_client() or hr_mock_client()) records a worker's calls in that worker's copy, which this process never sees; ask the trace, or the client's $calls(), instead.

delay_between_calls

Seconds to sleep between sequential calls, for rate-limit shaping. Honoured by map_reduce, refine and skim; the other readers do not sleep.

on_overflow

For stuff: "warn" (truncate and say so) or "error".

effort

How much a reasoning model reasons before it answers, or NULL (the default) to send nothing, so every request goes out at the provider's default exactly as before. One string, such as "low", applies to every call. A character vector named by stage sets it per stage: c(extract = "low", "synthesise.section" = "high"). A name covers each call whose trace label is that name or starts with it and a dot; the longest name that covers a label wins; an unnamed element, or one named "default", covers the labels no name does, and a label nothing covers is sent no effort. A name must cover a stem some registered reader, segmenter or stage declares (the calls column of gr_readers() and gr_segmenters()), or a label under one, so a misspelt name is an error of class hr_unknown_effort_key that lists the stems, not a setting that reaches no call. It reaches the segmenters that call a model too, when the spec is part of a recipe. See the section on reasoning effort.

premise

Check the question's assumptions against the document. A question can take for granted something the document contradicts ("Why did revenue fall?" of a report in which it rose). Without this check a reader answers it on its own terms or reports NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, and either way what the document does say is lost. With premise = TRUE the prompts that answer the question tell the model that, when the excerpts state the contrary of an assumption in it, it is to say so in one sentence giving what they state instead, rather than answer. That sentence becomes $answer and $premise (see gr_answer), and is_not_found() is FALSE for it. Excerpts that are merely silent are still NOT_IN_DOCUMENT. See "Checking the premise" below for how each reader combines what its requests report. The verdict is the model's reading of the excerpts, not a check harnessr makes, so weigh it as you would any answer. Off by default because it changes what is sent: the prompts are longer, so a cache, a recorded replay or a gr_read_many() store made without it does not answer a run with it, and the reverse. screen and extract, which answer no question, ignore it.

verify

Check the answer's quotations against the chunks they come from, and let the check decide what is accepted. FALSE (the default) sends the same requests and accepts answers as before; the quote_* shadow columns are still recorded on checked evidence (see "Verifying quotations"). With TRUE, gr_read() runs gr_verify_evidence() on every answer, writes its columns onto $evidence, marks the answer partial when a quotation is not found, and records a read.verify step in the trace. The iterative reader also asks each step that says it can answer for the passages it rests on, word for word with their chunk numbers, and stops only when every one is found in the chunk it names; a refused step is told which quotations were not found, and a run that ends with none accepted answers NOT_IN_DOCUMENT. Its evidence is then the quotations, not every chunk it was shown. A step that reports the premise false (premise = TRUE) is not asked for quotations and is not refused for lacking them: its verdict stops the loop as it does without verify. See "Verifying quotations" below.

accept_near_verbatim

Under verify = TRUE, whether a quotation the edit-distance matcher scores near_verbatim (see "Verifying quotations") also lets the iterative reader stop. FALSE (the default) accepts only a quotation the decisive check verifies, as before the setting existed. A near-verbatim quotation that stops the loop is still reported as not verified in $evidence, so the answer is marked partial. TRUE without verify = TRUE is refused with a gr_bad_setting error. Untested: nothing has measured whether accepting near-verbatim quotations gives better answers, and on the package's labelled quotation set 25 of 46 quotations with one content word swapped scored near_verbatim.

max_merge_levels

The most merge levels map_reduce, skim and the other readers that merge findings run before they give up and return the findings unmerged and cut, with the answer partial. [1, 12], default 6, the cap the code had before it was a setting. Separate from max_levels, which only hierarchical reads. Untested.

restate_tokens

Under restate = "auto", the length of the excerpts, in tokens, above which the question is repeated before them. [0, 1e6], default 1200, the value the code had before it was a setting. Untested: the code called it "a number, and an arbitrary one".

bm25_k1, bm25_b

The Okapi BM25 parameters of the word-matching scores that rerank prefilters its candidates with and that retrieve blends in when embeddings are lexical. Defaults 1.5 and 0.75, the usual values given by Robertson and Zaragoza (2009), "The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond"; not tuned on this package's tasks. bm25_k1 [0, 10], bm25_b [0, 1].

lexical_blend

For retrieve when the embeddings are lexical (the offline embedder, or the fallback when the embeddings request fails): the weight of the cosine score, with 1 - lexical_blend on the BM25 score. [0, 1], default 0.5, an even blend chosen when the offline path was written. Untested.

unskip_k

For preview: how many of the sections that match the question's words best (BM25 over each section's text) are read in full even when the plan skips them. A section that shares no word with the question is never unskipped. [0, 100], default 0, which follows the plan as before. With unskip_k = 1, a plan that skips the only section holding the question's words is overridden. Whatever its value, each section the plan skipped is logged in the trace as a preview.skip step with its score and whether it was unskipped, and notes$unskipped lists the sections it overrode. Untested.

reread_on

For preview: "never" (the default) or "not_found". Under "not_found", an answer request that came back NOT_IN_DOCUMENT is followed by one more (preview.reread) over the sections the plan did not have read in full (skipped, skimmed, or demoted for lack of room), fitted whole to one request in document order. The re-read's answer replaces the not-found when it finds one; notes$reread and a preview.reread trace step say what was sent and whether it found an answer. It costs at most one request. Untested.

low_score

For rerank, what happens when every candidate the model scored is below rerank_min_score. "not_found" (the default) makes no answer request and returns NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, as before, now with notes$retrieval_low_score = TRUE and a rerank.low_score trace step. "read_top_k" sends the 5 best-scored candidates to the answer request anyway (notes$read_below_min_score = TRUE), and marks a NOT_IN_DOCUMENT reply with notes$retrieval_low_score = TRUE. It costs the answer request the default does not make. Untested.

fusion

For retrieve and iterative: how the embedding ranking and the BM25 word-matching ranking are combined. Both readers rank through one function. "default" keeps each reader's 0.6.0 ranking: retrieve blends cosine with BM25 by lexical_blend when the embeddings are lexical and uses cosine alone otherwise, and iterative uses cosine alone, so on embeddings that are not lexical the two rank alike. "rrf" is reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher 2009, "Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual Rank Learning Methods"): each chunk scores the sum of 1 / (rrf_k + rank) over the two rankings, whatever the embeddings, and both readers fuse alike. It costs no request. Under "rrf", min_score applies to the fused score, which lies between 0 and 2 / (rrf_k + 1), about 0.033 at the default rrf_k: a floor chosen for cosine, such as 0.1, passes no chunk, so retrieve reads its best chunk alone and sets notes$below_min_score. With mmr below 1, the fused scores are rescaled to [0, 1] over the chunks still eligible before they are weighed against similarity, which lies between 0 and 1; the order, and so the plain top-k pick, is unchanged. Untested.

rrf_k

Under fusion = "rrf", the constant k. [1, 1e4], default 60, the value Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher (2009) use (cited); not tuned here. A larger k flattens the difference between top ranks.

answer_format

How the requests that answer the question report what they found. "parsed" (the default) sends the free-text requests sent before the setting existed and reads NOT_IN_DOCUMENT from the reply. "schema" sends them with a JSON schema that asks for answer and outcome ("answered" or "not_found"); a "not_found" reply becomes NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, and the model's own words go to notes$structured$reply. A reply that does not parse is read as free text (notes$structured$parsed = FALSE). It covers the answering request of stuff, retrieve, rerank, skim, hierarchical, preview and iterative's final answer, and each chunk's request of map_reduce; merges, refine's drafts, ensemble's adjudication and iterative's steps (already structured) are sent as before. Either way the answer's $outcome is set (see gr_answer). Untested: published comparisons of forced schemas and free text disagree, so the default stays "parsed" until a live comparison settles it.

premise_verdict

Under premise = TRUE, how a verdict is reported. "sentence" (the default) is the FALSE_PREMISE: sentence in the reply, as before. "structured" sends the answering requests that answer_format = "schema" covers with a JSON schema holding premise_status ("holds" or "contradicted") and quote, the passage of the excerpts that states the contrary, word for word. The quote is checked with the matcher gr_verify_evidence() uses, against the excerpts the request was shown. Where those are passages or summaries a model wrote (skim, hierarchical and the skimmed sections of preview), the quote must also be found in the document. The answer gains $premise_verdict (see gr_answer). In map_reduce a chunk's flag stands only when its quote is found in that chunk: a flag with no quote, or one not found, is dropped with the chunk's reply (notes$premise_dropped), and a verified one goes to the merge and sets notes$degradation to "premise_flagged". "structured" without premise = TRUE is refused with a gr_bad_setting error. Untested.

context_policy

NULL (the default), or an hr_context_policy() (or a named list of its arguments) that decides what a request keeps when its text does not fit. NULL keeps each reader's own cuts, which keep the start of what they cut. With a policy:

  • refine fits its state (draft or ledger) and the new excerpt into the input budget together, cutting the pieces the policy allows in the order it gives, in place of giving each half the budget;

  • the merges of map_reduce and skim (findings), the summaries hierarchical combines (summaries), the outline and skimmed sections of preview (outline, excerpts) and the joined findings of a merge that gives up are cut with the policy's keep rule for that piece. These pieces have no scores, so the readers read a "scored" rule as "head";

  • the readers that pack whole chunks (stuff, retrieve, rerank, preview, iterative) write a "truncate" step naming the chunks they left out;

  • with order_merges = TRUE, the findings a merge combines and the member answers ensemble adjudicates are placed by context_order. The question and the instructions are never cut by any reader. When the pieces the policy pins do not fit a request, the reader warns once (class gr_context_policy_unfit) and cuts as it does without a policy, so the request still fits. Every cut is a "truncate" step of the trace that names the piece and the part dropped. Untested.

refine_state

For refine: what is carried down the document. "draft" (the default) is the answer, rewritten by each request, as before. "ledger" is a numbered list of findings: each request is shown it and one excerpt and replies with edits (ADD: <finding>, REPLACE <n>: <finding>, DROP <n>), which the code applies, so a finding no edit names is carried forward word for word and a corrected one is replaced rather than annotated. One more request, refine.answer, answers from the finished list; an empty list is NOT_IN_DOCUMENT with no request. notes$ledger_items counts the findings. Untested; gr_condensation_check() builds the test.

effort_mode

"static" (the default) sends each request at the effort effort names, as before. "escalate" starts every stage at effort ("low" when effort is unset) and sends the next stage at "high" when a trigger fired in the one before: a cut (a "truncate" step, or a reply stopped at its cap), a reply that is not the JSON asked for or does not fit its schema, NOT_IN_DOCUMENT from every request of the stage, a quotation iterative could not verify, or ensemble members that disagree. Effort changes only at a stage boundary, at most once a read, and the stage after a raised one goes back to effort. The spec's effort is then an hr_effort_escalate() policy; each raise is an "effort.escalate" step of the trace, whether it resolved the trigger an "effort.resolve" step, and hr_effort_log() lists both. hr_effort_check() compares it with fixed levels. Untested.

...

Extra fields for custom readers.

Value

A list of class gr_read_spec.

Checking the premise

With premise = TRUE, every request that answers the question carries the rule: the single answering request of stuff, retrieve, rerank, skim, hierarchical and preview; each chunk's request and the merge of map_reduce; the draft and every revision of refine; each step and the final answer of iterative; and the adjudication of ensemble. Requests that only pick, score, summarise or copy out passages do not.

map_reduce treats a chunk that contradicts the premise differently from one that only lacks the answer. The second is dropped, as it always was. The first is passed to the merge as a finding that says the premise is contradicted and what the excerpt states instead, and the merge, told the same rule, weighs it against the chunks that did answer and may itself report the premise false. notes$premise_chunks lists the chunks that reported it, whatever the merge decided. ensemble does the same with its members (notes$premise_members). refine carries the verdict in its draft, so a later excerpt can add to the correction or overturn it. iterative's step reports it in a false_premise field of its reply, which is in the schema only when the premise is checked, and stops there. A merge or adjudication that failed returns the findings joined, which is no verdict: $premise is NA, and the notes still name the chunks or members that reported it.

The answer records the check: $premise is NA when nothing contradicted the question, and the correction when something did. gr_compare() and gr_read_many() add a premise column to their summaries, print() and gr_audit_report() say when the model reported the premise false, and the trace has a read.premise step with the outcome.

Verifying quotations

A reader that puts the chunks it read into $evidence has quoted them by construction, so for stuff, retrieve, rerank and the default iterative a passing check says only that the chunks were the ones sent. The check means something where a model chose what to quote: skim, extract, screen, and iterative under verify = TRUE.

Two matchers score each quotation. The one that decides verified is the check described in gr_verify_evidence(), unchanged. Beside it the answer carries quote_status, quote_sim, quote_coverage, quote_edits and quote_critical_ok from an edit-distance matcher that tolerates ligatures, line-break hyphens and OCR letter errors while requiring numbers, units and negations to be identical. It is recorded only, and decides nothing in this release.

verify = TRUE changes what iterative sends (its schema and instructions), so a cache or recording made without it does not answer a run with it. The other readers send exactly what they sent before.

Out-of-range values

Numeric arguments are clamped into a usable range and the change is warned about, never applied silently: top_k [1, 1e4], fan_in [2, 32], max_levels [1, 12], max_rounds [1, 20], rerank_candidates [1, 1e4], rerank_min_score [0, 10], preview_tokens [100, 1e5], delay_between_calls [0, 600], token caps [16, 1e6]. The ranges of the settings added later are given with each argument.

Where the defaults come from

Each setting's default, its tier (basic for the few most users change, advanced for the rest) and the evidence behind the value. untested means no measurement backs the value; cited names the published source it comes from. The settings added as declared parameters (accept_near_verbatim, max_merge_levels, restate_tokens, bm25_k1, bm25_b, lexical_blend, and the reading options added after them) are stored in the spec only when they are not their default, so a default spec keeps the store and cache keys it had before they existed.

  • on_overflow (default "warn", advanced): untested. Chosen so that a document too long for one request still gets an answer that says what was cut.

  • context_order (default "relevance", advanced): untested. The order the readers used before the setting existed; the alternatives were added to be compared, and no comparison is recorded.

  • restate (default "auto", advanced): untested. A setting so that gr_compare() can measure it on a corpus; no measurement is recorded.

  • premise (default FALSE, advanced): untested. Off, so a run sends the requests it sent before the check existed.

  • verify (default FALSE, basic): untested. Off, so a run sends the requests and accepts the answers it did before the check existed.

  • effort (default NULL, advanced): untested. Unset: no effort is sent, and the provider's own default applies.

  • reader (default "map_reduce", basic): untested. The reader that sends every chunk, chosen because it reads the whole document at any length; no comparison of readers is recorded.

  • model (default NULL, basic): untested. Not a tuned value: NULL takes the client's model.

  • temperature (default NULL, advanced): untested. Not a tuned value: NULL takes hr_options("temperature"), which sends none.

  • max_answer_tokens (default 1500, advanced): untested. Set as a generous cap for an answer; not measured.

  • max_chunk_tokens (default 700, advanced): untested. Set as a cap for one chunk's finding; not measured.

  • max_summary_tokens (default 500, advanced): untested. Set as a cap for one summary; not measured.

  • top_k (default 6, basic): untested. A common starting value for retrieval; not tuned here.

  • min_score (default -Inf, advanced): untested. Not a tuned value: -Inf applies no floor.

  • mmr (default 1, advanced): untested. 1 is plain top-k, the selection used before the setting existed.

  • rerank_candidates (default 20, advanced): untested. Set when rerank was written; not tuned.

  • rerank_min_score (default 4, advanced): untested. Set when rerank was written; not tuned.

  • fan_in (default 5, advanced): untested. Set when hierarchical was written; not tuned.

  • max_levels (default 5, advanced): untested. Set when hierarchical was written; not tuned.

  • max_rounds (default 4, advanced): untested. Set when iterative was written; not tuned.

  • preview_tokens (default 1200, advanced): untested. Set when preview was written; not tuned.

  • members (default NULL, advanced): untested. NULL takes ensemble's own pair, retrieve and map_reduce; not compared with other pairs.

  • cite (default FALSE, basic): untested. Off, so the answer prompt is the one used before the setting existed.

  • skim_model (default NULL, advanced): untested. Not a tuned value: NULL uses model.

  • summary_model (default NULL, advanced): untested. Not a tuned value: NULL uses model.

  • parallel (default NULL, advanced): untested. Not a tuned value: NULL follows hr_options("parallel"). It does not change output.

  • delay_between_calls (default 0, advanced): untested. No pause. It does not change output.

  • accept_near_verbatim (default FALSE, advanced): untested. Off, as the code behaved before the setting existed. Not measured as a stopping rule; on the labelled quotation set, 25 of 46 quotations with one content word swapped score near_verbatim (NEWS, 0.6.0.9000).

  • max_merge_levels (default 6, advanced): untested. The cap the merge code had as a constant; not tuned.

  • restate_tokens (default 1200, advanced): untested. An arbitrary number, as its comment said when it was a constant; not measured.

  • bm25_k1 (default 1.5, advanced): cited. Robertson and Zaragoza (2009), "The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond", give k1 between 1.2 and 2.0 as usual; not tuned here.

  • bm25_b (default 0.75, advanced): cited. Robertson and Zaragoza (2009), "The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond", give b = 0.75 as usual; not tuned here.

  • lexical_blend (default 0.5, advanced): untested. An even blend, set when the offline path was written.

  • unskip_k (default 0, advanced): untested. Off (0), so the plan is followed as it was before the setting existed. Not measured.

  • reread_on (default "never", advanced): untested. "never", so a run makes the requests it made before the setting existed. Not measured.

  • low_score (default "not_found", advanced): untested. "not_found", the behaviour before the setting existed: no answer request. Not measured.

  • fusion (default "default", advanced): untested. "default" keeps the 0.6.0 ranking of each reader. Reciprocal rank fusion is not compared with it here.

  • rrf_k (default 60, advanced): cited. Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher (2009), "Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual Rank Learning Methods", SIGIR, use k = 60; not tuned here.

  • answer_format (default "parsed", advanced): untested. "parsed", the requests sent before the setting existed. Published comparisons of forced schemas and free text disagree; owner decision DEC-05 keeps the question open until a live comparison.

  • premise_verdict (default "sentence", advanced): untested. "sentence", the requests premise = TRUE sent before the setting existed. Not measured.

  • context_policy (default NULL, advanced): untested. NULL: each reader cuts as it did before the setting existed, keeping the start of what it cuts. No policy has been compared with it.

  • refine_state (default "draft", advanced): untested. "draft", the state refine carried before the setting existed. Not compared with "ledger"; gr_condensation_check() builds the test.

  • effort_mode (default "static", advanced): untested. "static": the effort effort names, as before the setting existed. Not compared with "escalate"; hr_effort_check() makes the comparison.

Reasoning effort

The default models reason before they write a reply, and that reasoning is billed as output and counted against the same output cap as the reply. Nothing sets how much unless effort does, so a corpus's hundreds of per-chunk calls reason as long as the one call that drafts its claims.

The effort is sent as reasoning = {"effort": ...} on the Responses API and as reasoning_effort on Chat Completions, and an hr_mock_client() or hr_backend_client() handler finds it in params$effort. It is sent only to a model whose hr_model_info() says reasoning = TRUE, and left out without a warning for any other, which would refuse the field, as temperature is left out for a model that refuses that; register a gateway's reasoning model with hr_register_model() to reach it. For the calls it covers it replaces an effort the client's extra_body sets. An hr_ellmer_client() cannot take it per call, says so once (gr_effort_unsupported) and does not record it as sent. A value is passed through as given; one that is not "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high" or "xhigh" is warned about (gr_effort_unknown) and sent anyway, since providers add levels.

Each request's effort is in its trace step (params$effort, and an effort column of as.data.frame(trace)), and gr_audit_report() shows it beside what each stage cost. It is part of the hr_cache() key, and, when set, of a recipe's store key in gr_read_many(), of what gr_compare() counts as a different recipe, and of the key an hr_replay_client() matches on, so runs at different efforts never share answers. Unset, none of those keys change.

The labels are the stage column of as.data.frame(trace): segment.context, segment.proposition; stuff.answer; map.answer, reduce; refine.draft, refine.revise, refine.answer; skim.extract, skim.consolidate, skim.answer; retrieve.answer; rerank.score, rerank.answer; hier.summarise.L1 (and L2, ...), hier.answer; iterative.step, iterative.final; ensemble.adjudicate; preview.plan, preview.skim, preview.answer; screen.decide; extract.chunk, extract.resolve; and, for gr_claims(), gr_outline() and gr_synthesise(), claims.draw, claims.reconcile, outline.derive, synthesise.section, synthesise.batch, synthesise.merge and synthesise.revise.structure (.cut, .register). A merge that takes more than one level labels the levels below its final merge .level1, .level2 and so on, which its own name covers.

A starting point, not a default: low for the many mechanical calls and high for the few that judge.

effort = c("extract.chunk" = "low", "skim.extract" = "low",
           "rerank.score" = "low", segment = "low", "map.answer" = "low",
           "claims.draw" = "high", "outline.derive" = "high",
           "synthesise.section" = "high", "ensemble.adjudicate" = "high")

Reasoning shares the reply's cap, so a call at "high" can spend all of it and come back cut off (finish_reason = "length", warned about where it matters). Give such stages room: max_answer_tokens here, max_section_tokens in gr_synthesise(), max_outline_tokens in gr_outline(). Requests to a reasoning model are sent with an output cap of at least 2048 tokens whatever the effort, and the cost limits are checked at that cap.

See also

gr_readers() for the available readers and their call costs, gr_read(), gr_recipe()

Other reading functions: gr_answer, gr_check_reader(), gr_methods_text(), gr_read(), gr_reader_signature(), gr_readers(), gr_register_reader(), gr_step(), is_not_found(), new_answer()

Examples

gr_read_spec("retrieve", top_k = 8)$top_k
#> [1] 8

# Out-of-range settings are corrected loudly, not quietly.
suppressWarnings(gr_read_spec("hierarchical", fan_in = 999)$fan_in)
#> [1] 32

# Reasoning effort by stage: little for the per-chunk calls, more for the
# merge. The trace says which request carried which.
ch <- gr_segment(gr_example(), list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 150))
#> Using cached ingestion for this document + settings.
#> Segmenting with 'paragraph' (cap 150 tokens, overlap 0).
cl <- hr_mock_client(function(m, p) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")
sp <- gr_read_spec("map_reduce", model = "gpt-5.6-luna",
                   effort = c(map = "low", reduce = "high"))
tr <- hr_trace()
invisible(gr_read(ch, "What was revenue?", cl, sp, trace = tr))
#> Reading with 'map_reduce' (all|N+logN|tree) over 5 chunk(s).
unique(as.data.frame(tr)[, c("stage", "effort")])
#>        stage effort
#> 1 map.answer    low
#> 6     reduce   high
# A loaded question, checked against the document. The mock plays a model
# that finds the excerpts contradict it.
cl <- hr_mock_client(function(m, p)
  "FALSE_PREMISE: Revenue rose 12% in 2023, to 45.2 million.")
ch <- gr_segment(gr_example(), list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 400))
#> Using cached ingestion for this document + settings.
#> Segmenting with 'sentence' (cap 400 tokens, overlap 0).
ans <- gr_read(ch, "Why did revenue fall in 2023?", cl,
               gr_read_spec("stuff", premise = TRUE))
#> Reading with 'stuff' (all|1|none) over 2 chunk(s).
ans$premise
#> [1] "Revenue rose 12% in 2023, to 45.2 million."
is_not_found(ans$answer)
#> [1] FALSE
